cases.reference: Viterbi decoding uses dynamic programming to find the most likely sequence.
cases.correct: The algorithm finds the best state sequence by storing the optimal previous state at every step.
cases.incorrect_similar: Viterbi decoding greedily picks the most likely state at each step independently to find the sequence.

cases.reference: TF-IDF weights a word by its term frequency multiplied by its inverse document frequency; words such as 'the' that appear in most documents are down-weighted, while rare, discriminative words receive a higher weight.
cases.correct: Words found in nearly every text carry little information, so their importance is pushed towards zero, while terms specific to a few texts are emphasised.
cases.incorrect_similar: TF-IDF gives the highest weight to words that appear in most documents, because the inverse document frequency grows with the document frequency.

cases.reference: Cosine similarity is the dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their norms; it depends only on direction, so it is insensitive to document length, unlike Euclidean distance.
cases.correct: It looks at the angle between the two document vectors rather than how far apart their tips are, so a long and a short document on the same subject still come out close.
cases.incorrect_similar: Cosine similarity divides the Euclidean distance by the dot product, so it depends heavily on document length.

cases.reference: Maximum likelihood gives zero probability to bigrams never seen in training; add-one (Laplace) smoothing adds one to every count and the vocabulary size to the denominator so no probability is zero.
cases.correct: If a word pair never showed up in the training text the model would call any sentence containing it impossible, so we pretend every pair was seen one extra time.
cases.incorrect_similar: Add-one smoothing adds one to the vocabulary size so that frequent bigrams get a higher probability than in maximum likelihood.

cases.reference: Perplexity is the inverse probability of the test text normalised by the number of words; a lower perplexity means a better language model.
cases.correct: It is two raised to the per-token cross-entropy, so the less surprised the model is by held-out text, the smaller the value and the better the model.
cases.incorrect_similar: Perplexity is the inverse probability of the test text normalised by the number of words; a higher perplexity means a better language model.
